title: Surge pool provisioning, temporary boost API, and overage billing behavior
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Background: Enterprise customers using Dedicated capacity have requested controlled burst behavior during traffic spikes. Current autoscaling grants more instances but can take several minutes, leading to missed latency SLAs. We want a predictable, auditable 'burst' capability that: (1) provides a short-lived boost of capacity via surge pools, (2) exposes a Temporary Boost API for programmatic triggers, and (3) defines clear overage billing rules and visibility in the Console.

Goals: Create a burst-capacity surface that satisfies three constraints:
- Predictable performance: emergency short-lived throughput guarantees for pinned tenants (e.g., 1–15 min).
- Cost control: clear pricing model for bursts (flat surcharge + per-second usage) and protections against runaway consumption.
- Operational safety: admission control, fair-share across customers, and ability to revoke boosts automatically.

Scope & features:
1) Surge pool concept and runtime integration:
   - Provision a managed pool of warm GPU workers in each region (surge pools) that can be attached to a customer's fleet for short windows.
   - Surge pools are separate from reserved Dedicated nodes to avoid impacting committed capacity.
   - Backend: admission controller in the router to allocate a customer's burst tokens from the nearest pool based on routing policy. Uses KV cache-friendly warm processes for < startup_time 30s.

2) Temporary Boost API:
   - POST /v1/dedicated/:fleet_id/boosts to request N tokens for T seconds with optional max_price and priority_hint.
   - Response includes boost_id, estimated activation_time, granted_tokens, and billing_terms link.
   - Quotas: per-customer concurrent boosts limit and daily burst-second cap.

3) Overage billing and invoicing behavior:
   - Billing model: base surcharge (per-boost) + per-burst-second rate tiered by token-size and region.
   - Grace window: first 30s of a boost are billed at 50% of standard burst rate to encourage short spikes.
   - Auto-throttle: if a customer exceeds a soft budget threshold, further boosts are denied and an email/SMS alert is sent to billing contacts.

4) Console & observability:
   - New Console panels: Active boosts, Burst spending forecast (hourly), and a per-boost timeline with latency/throughput overlays.
   - Audit logs for every boost request and automatic revocations.

5) Safety & fairness policies:
   - Preemption: boosts are revocable when pool pressure rises; we implement staggered preemption with graceful fallback to narrower model variant.
   - Fair-share algorithm: weighted by subscription tier and recent usage; documented percent floor for enterprise customers.

Non-goals: providing unbounded capacity, replacing long-term autoscaling behaviors for baseline throughput, or offering free unlimited bursts for trial accounts.

Acceptance criteria:
- Feature parity: Temporary Boost API implemented + tested in staging with 3 regions.
- Billing: Billing engine can rate a boost (surcharge + per-second), emit usage records, and surface estimates in Console.
- Runtime: activation latency 95th <= 30s for warm pools, and 99th <= 90s for cold pools.
- Safety: automatic revoke logic triggers under pool pressure and does not cause silent request loss (fallbacks/queued requests).
- Docs: API spec, Console mockups, support playbook, and customer FAQ published.

Implementation notes:
- Runtime: reuse existing warm-start worker image with a light pre-warming hook to populate KV caches. Add admission controller endpoint in routing plane to check and deduct per-boost tokens.
- Autoscaler: treat surge pools as an orthogonal pool managed by a new controller (surge-controller) with its own scaling policies tied to provider-spot quotas.
- Billing pipeline: emit BOOST_USAGE events to the existing usage-events topic; extend billing lambda to apply surcharge rules and grace-window logic.
- API: version Temporary Boost API as v1-beta and gate with feature-flag until rollout 50% of customers.

Testing & rollout plan:
- Stage 1 (dev/staging): unit tests, integration test with billing simulator, chaos injection to validate preemption paths.
- Stage 2 (canary): enable for internal customers and a set of opt-in customers; monitor boost latency, revenue delta, and incidents.
- Stage 3 (GA): enable via Console toggle + default quotas.

Customer communication:
- Pre-GA: outreach to top 20 dedicated customers for feedback.
- GA release notes: include pricing examples, limits, and migration steps.

Risks & mitigations:
- Cost surprises: provide conservative default quotas and require billing contact opt-in for high budgets.
- Provider limits: surge pool controllers will be region-aware and prefer burst in regions with available spot capacity.
- SLA disputes: add explicit SLO scope to contracts — bursts reduce guaranteed baseline SLO but have separate burst SLAs.
acceptance_criteria: 1) API documented and implemented; 2) Billing records produced for every boost and surfaced in Console; 3) Activation latency meets 95th<=30s for warm pools; 4) Preemption path validated under synthetic load; 5) Audit logs retained and searchable; 6) Feature-flagged rollout completed for canary customers.
implementation_notes: See design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Surge+Pools+Design and prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/2314. Key infra changes: surge-controller service, admission-controller route, BOOST_USAGE topic, boost-quotas table in billing-db.
